introduction: A comparison scene interrupts Cyrus’s expedition. In Plato’s Laches, Socrates discusses courage with the generals Laches and Nicias in a conversation about education. Xenophon is not a participant or an eyewitness in this scene.

Course adaptation of Plato, Laches 190e–192d. The initial definition, fighting during retreat, courage outside battle, and the question about endurance follow the passage. All Greek dialogue below is newly simplified course wording; the frame and transitions are supplied. This selection does not solve the whole dialogue’s inquiry.

Read present active participles as descriptions of people acting at the same time as the main verb. Blue glosses support names, contracted forms, and less familiar words. The final question will matter when soldiers refuse to march and later retreat.

Ὁ Λάχης λέγει· «ὁ ἐν τῇ τάξει μένων καὶ πρὸς τοὺς πολεμίους μαχόμενος ἀνδρεῖός ἐστιν. οὗτος οὐ φεύγει, ἀλλὰ τοὺς φίλους σῴζει.» ὁ Σωκράτης τὸν λέγοντα βλέπει.

reading.translation:
Socrates, Laches, and Nicias discuss courage. Socrates asks, “What is courage?” Laches listens and considers the soldiers in battle.

Laches says, “The man remaining in his position and fighting against the enemies is brave. He does not flee but saves his friends.” Socrates watches the speaker.

Socrates asks, “And what of those fleeing? The Scythians fight both while fleeing and while pursuing. The retreating horsemen are not all cowardly.” Laches agrees about the horsemen.

Socrates also speaks about the Spartans: “The retreating soldiers fight again.” Laches accepts the example. For not only those remaining but also those retreating appear brave.

Socrates does not ask only about war. “The person bearing illness, the person living in poverty, and the person speaking in the city often face dangers. What do brave people have in common?”

Laches speaks again: “Courage is a kind of endurance.” Socrates asks, “Is all endurance good? Endurance with judgment is good; but what of endurance without judgment?” The listeners consider the question.

The discussion still proceeds; those conversing do not stop investigating. Laches admires the man remaining in his position, while Socrates also examines his judgment. Does the person persisting always act rightly?

wordStudy.label: Word Study — Courage, persistence, and judgment

blocks.title: Courage, persistence, and judgment
body: ἀνδρεία names courage; ἀνδρεῖος describes a brave person. The related adjective agrees with its noun, while the abstract noun can stand as the subject of a definition. A battlefield example is a παράδειγμα, not yet a definition covering every case.

μένω means remain; καρτερέω means persist, and καρτερία is endurance. These words overlap in a scene but are not interchangeable: μένω describes staying, while καρτερέω emphasizes bearing difficulty. φρόνησις adds judgment to the discussion.

Compare φεύγω, flee, διώκω, pursue, and ὑποχωρέω, retreat. The participles identify what a person is doing. The ethical question concerns the purpose and judgment of that action, rather than a rule that a single movement always proves courage.

sections.title: 1. Forming Present Active Participles
body: A present active participle describes someone or something engaged in an action. Start with the present stem: λυ- in λύω. Masculine nominative singular is λύων, feminine λύουσα, neuter λῦον. The three gender forms belong to one participle, not three finite verbs.

The underlying masculine/neuter stem is λυοντ-. Feminine forms use λυουσ- and first-declension endings. From μένω form μένων, μένουσα, μένον; from φεύγω form φεύγων, φεύγουσα, φεῦγον. Contraction produces ὑποχωρῶν, ὑποχωροῦσα, ὑποχωροῦν.

Recognize the gender form before translating. λέγων means speaking (masculine singular), not “he speaks”: the finite form is λέγει. Supplementary feminine and neuter examples teach the complete pattern without inventing participants in Plato’s scene.

examples.english: The woman remains while speaking (supplementary example).

checks.answer: μένουσα. The feminine nominative singular uses -ουσα.

checks.prompt: Which is neuter nominative singular of λύω’s participle?
checks.answer: λῦον. The neuter singular is λῦον.

sections.title: 2. Declining -ων, -ουσα, -ον
body: The masculine and neuter use third-declension endings on an -οντ- stem. In λύοντος, λύοντι, λύοντα the ντ remains visible. The masculine nominative singular λύων has lost the final τ; neuter λῦον has the same form in nominative and accusative.

In the dative plural, ντ disappears before σ and the preceding vowel lengthens: λυοντ-σι becomes λύουσι(ν). This participial form can look like the finite third-person plural. The article and sentence structure distinguish τοῖς λύουσι, “to those releasing,” from λύουσι, “they release.”

The feminine declines like a first-declension noun in short α: λύουσα, λυούσης, λυούσῃ, λύουσαν. Learn the accents with the forms. The genitive and dative singular move the accent because the ending is long.

sections.title: 3. Finding the Person Described
body: Participles agree in gender, number, and case with the noun or pronoun they describe. In οἱ ὑποχωροῦντες ἱππεῖς, article, participle, and noun are masculine nominative plural. All identify the retreating horsemen as the subject.

Agreement is grammatical rather than a word-order rule. In ὁ Λάχης ἀκούων σκέπτεται, ἀκούων belongs to Laches even though the main verb follows it. In τὸν λέγοντα the article shows masculine accusative singular, identifying the object of watching.

Do not attach every nearby participle to the closest name. Read its ending and compare possible nouns. Supplementary ἡ γυνὴ λέγουσα and τὰ παιδία παίζοντα show feminine singular and neuter plural agreement.

φεύγοντες. The masculine nominative plural agrees with ἱππεῖς.

sections.title: 4. Describing, Naming, and Adding Circumstances
body: An attributive participle stands with the article and noun: οἱ ὑποχωροῦντες ἱππεῖς, “the retreating horsemen.” It limits which horsemen are meant, like an adjective. A second attributive position is οἱ ἱππεῖς οἱ ὑποχωροῦντες.

A substantival participle uses an article with no expressed noun: οἱ φεύγοντες, “those fleeing”; τὸν λέγοντα, “the speaker.” Supply “person” or “people” as needed. The ending still carries gender, number, and case.

A simple circumstantial participle adds an accompanying action: ἀκούων σκέπτεται, “while listening, he considers.” Unlike an attributive phrase it does not specify a separate group. Contrast active ἀκούων with middle μαχόμενος or διαλεγόμενοι from Lesson 15: both decline and agree, but the voice forms differ.

sections.title: 5. Ongoing Action with a Main Verb
body: The present participle presents an action as ongoing, normally simultaneous with the main verb in these simple examples. ἀκούων σκέπτεται combines listening and considering in one scene. It does not report one completed action followed by another.

The participle does not independently identify the time of the whole sentence. Our main verbs are present, so “while listening, he considers” is a natural translation. Later lessons will combine present participles with past main verbs; that does not change the participle’s ongoing aspect.

Distinguish syntax from moral inference. φεύγοντες μάχονται says that the people fight while fleeing. It does not prove that every flight is brave. The question whether καρτερία requires judgment remains open as this selection closes.

sections.title: An example is not a complete definition
body: Plato frames this discussion around the education of young men and the value of military training. Laches and Nicias have military standing, while Socrates tests what their claims actually cover. The selection begins with Laches’s familiar soldier who holds his place. That is intelligible as an example of courage, but an example need not include every courageous act.

Socrates does not simply declare the example false. He accepts that such a soldier can be brave and asks whether courage also appears elsewhere. This is a model of critical inquiry: a counterexample tests the breadth of a claim. The course frame places the three named speakers in Plato’s conversation; it does not insert Xenophon into the cast.

sections.title: Retreat and the purpose of movement
body: At Laches 191a–c Socrates mentions Scythian horsemen and a reported Spartan maneuver at Plataea. Fighting during withdrawal or turning after retreat challenges the claim that staying physically still is necessary for courage. The reading summarizes those examples in present Greek instead of reproducing Plato’s complex narrative.

This tactical comparison matters to Cyrus’s expedition because movement away from danger will later be unavoidable. It does not mean any retreat is wise. The source offers cases to examine, and the learner must ask what a movement accomplishes, who benefits, and whether the people making it have good reasons.

sections.title: Endurance and judgment
body: At 191d Socrates extends the inquiry to danger at sea, illness, poverty, and civic affairs, as well as fears and desires. The lesson selects illness, poverty, and public speaking to keep the Greek manageable. Courage becomes a question about facing difficulty across several parts of life.

Laches’s next proposal makes courage a kind of endurance. By 192d Socrates is distinguishing endurance with judgment from endurance without it. The dialogue continues beyond this excerpt. Our closing question invites comparison with leaders and soldiers; it does not announce a definition that Plato’s whole discussion has conclusively established.

questions.prompt: Why is Laches’s first example insufficient as a definition?
questions.answer: It may identify a brave soldier without covering brave actions in other circumstances.

questions.prompt: Does Socrates say that every retreat is courageous?
questions.answer: No. His examples show that staying still is not a necessary condition; context and judgment remain relevant.

questions.prompt: Why include illness and poverty?
questions.answer: They broaden the inquiry beyond military action, as Plato does at 191d.

questions.prompt: Is Xenophon present in the reading?
questions.answer: No. This is a separate adapted scene from Plato, not an expedition conversation.

questions.prompt: Does the excerpt resolve the dialogue?
questions.answer: No. It ends with a question about endurance and judgment.

questions.prompt: How might the discussion affect a judgment about refusing orders?
questions.answer: It encourages examining reasons and consequences instead of treating persistence or obedience alone as proof of courage.

questions.prompt: Which leadership decision in this lesson needs reasons beyond personal bravery?
questions.answer: Remaining or retreating needs a judgment about what the movement accomplishes.

questions.prompt: How can the reading’s source boundary improve your interpretation?
questions.answer: Distinguish the author’s reported events and speeches from the course’s simplified wording, supplied examples, and ethical inferences.
